Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) alleged that he and several associates had been part of a doping conspiracy that began in the late 1990s. According to USADA, Armstrong used performance-enhancing drugs—including [erythropoietin](https://www.britannica.com/science/erythropoietin) (EPO) and [human growth hormone](https://www.britannica.com/science/growth-hormone) —and underwent blood transfusions and [testosterone](https://www.britannica.com/science/testosterone) injections. After being stripped of his Tour titles, Armstrong continued to proclaim his innocence until 2013, when he admitted to taking performance-enhancing drugs.

### How much do the Tour de France winners get paid?

The total winnings for the 2025 [Tour de France](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Tour-de-France) were about €2.5 million ($2.9 million). The winner received €500,000 ($587,000). The second-place finisher was awarded €200,000 ($235,000), while the rider in third place got €100,000 ($117,500).
Others receiving cash awards include the stage winners, each of whom is paid 11,000 ($13,000). (Conversion rates are approximate.)

### Who has been stripped of a Tour de France title?

Five riders have been stripped of their Tour de France titles: Maurice Garin (1904), Bjarne Riis (1996), [Alberto Contador](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Alberto-Contador) (2010), [Lance Armstrong](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lance-Armstrong) (1999–2005), and Floyd Landis (2006). While Riis, Contador, Armstrong, and Landis were accused of taking performance-enhancing drugs, Garin had his title revoked for cheating. Although what Garin actually did is uncertain, the 1904 Tour was marred by numerous allegations of cheating. These included riders taking trains, being pulled by cars, and placing tacks on the road for rivals. In the end, the top four finishers were among those disqualified.

It is one of the most grueling events in all of [sports](https://www.britannica.com/sports/sports) .
Over the span of about 20 days, [Tour de France](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Tour-de-France) cyclists cover some 3,600 km (2,235 miles) of both flat land and great stretches of mountainous [inclines](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/inclines) . The annual race’s most difficult section is known as the “circle of death.” The rare cyclist who can perform well at both time trials and climbing usually ends up wearing the yellow jersey ( _maillot jaune_ ) of victory. The first Tour was held in 1903, and 60 cyclists competed, though only 21 finished. Maurice Garin of France was the winner.

While cheating has marred the Tour from the start, in recent years the race has been especially tarnished by allegations of illegal [drug use](https://www.britannica.com/topic/drug-use) . Several winners have been stripped of their titles, most notably [Lance Armstrong](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lance-Armstrong) , who was the first rider to capture seven titles.

  [Chris Froome](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Chris-Froome/Introduction) is a Kenyan-born British cyclist, most known as a four-time winner of the Tour de France (2013, 2015, 2016, and 2017).
In 2017, he became the first British rider to win the Vuelta a España, and the first rider in nearly four decades to win that race and the Tour de France in the same year. In May 2018, Froome won the Giro d’Italia, becoming the third cyclist to win the three Grand Tours consecutively. In Olympic competition, Froome won consecutive bronze medals in the men’s time trial at the 2012 London Games and the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Games.

**Chris Froome** (born May 20, 1985, Nairobi, Kenya) is a Kenyan-born British [cyclist](https://www.britannica.com/sports/cycling) who was a four-time winner of the [Tour de France](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Tour-de-France) (2013, 2015, 2016, and 2017).

Froome was born in [Nairobi](https://www.britannica.com/place/Nairobi) to British parents who later divorced when his father filed for [bankruptcy](https://www.britannica.com/money/bankruptcy) .

...

com/dictionary/designated) leader of Team Sky that year. He won the Tour de France again in 2015. Because of his consistently high level of performance, questions were raised about the possibility of his having used performance-enhancing drugs. In an effort to allay such suspicions, Froome released the results of his physiological tests following the 2015 Tour. The next year Froome became the first Tour de France winner in more than two decades to successfully defend his title—despite crashing twice, having to sprint uphill on foot when his bike was damaged in an accident, and engaging in a daredevil downhill attack as he lay prone atop his handlebars in an aero position.

In 2017 Froome ran his streak of consecutive Tour de France titles to three with his closest margin of victory (54 seconds) in that event. Later that year he became the first British rider to win the [Vuelta a España](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Vuelta-a-Espana) .
He also was the first rider in nearly four decades to win that race and the Tour de France in the same year. However, he failed a drug test during the Vuelta a España after his urine was found to have had double the permitted amount of the asthma drug salbutamol. Froome claimed that while he had increased the dosage when his asthma worsened, he had not [surpassed](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/surpassed) the allowable amount. An investigation was subsequently launched during which Froome was allowed to continue competing. He continued to make history in May 2018 when he won the Giro d’Italia (Tour of Italy), becoming the third cyclist to win the three Grand Tours consecutively. Two months later the doping case against Froome was dropped.

In June 2019, while competing in the Critérium du Dauphiné in France, Froome was involved in a serious crash that resulted in numerous injuries, including a broken hip.
He did not return to racing until February 2020, when he participated in the UAE Tour. That event, however, was canceled mid-race because of the [COVID-19](https://www.britannica.com/science/COVID-19) [pandemic](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/pandemic) . In 2021 he left Team Sky for Israel Start-Up Nation (now NSN Cycling) but struggled to perform to his previous standard. He retired in 2026, having last competed in a race the previous year.

## History

[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Tour_de_France_general_classification_winners&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History") ]

The [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France") was established in 1903 by the newspaper _[L'Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Auto "L'Auto")_ , in an attempt to increase its sales. The first race was won by Frenchman [Maurice Garin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Garin "Maurice Garin") .
He won again the next year, but was disqualified after allegations that he had been transported by car or rail. [Henri Cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Cornet "Henri Cornet") became the winner after the dispute was settled, and is the youngest to win the Tour. Following the scandals in 1904, the scoring system was changed from being time-based to a point-based system, in which the cyclist who has the fewest points at the end of the race is victorious. This system lasted until [1912](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Tour_de_France "1912 Tour de France") , when the time-based system was reintroduced. French cyclists won the first six Tours, before [François Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/François_Faber "François Faber") of Luxembourg won in [1909](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1909_Tour_de_France "1909 Tour de France") , the first non-Frenchman to win.. The Tour de France is world's biggest cycling race. Over the years, many riders have claimed victory and worn the yellow jersey, from the oldest to the youngest.

## Who has won the most Tour de France titles?

The record for most Tour de France victories is five, and it’s shared by four riders.
Jacques Anquetil was the first five-time winner, claiming the race in 1957, 1961, 1962, 1963 and 1964. He surpassed the previous record of three wins, which was held at the time by Philippe Thys and Louison Bobet.

Eddy Merckx equalled Anquetil’s haul, winning the Tour in 1969, 1970, 1971, 1972 and 1974. He skipped the 1973 edition to win the Vuelta a España and Giro d’Italia, and he was prevented from winning a record sixth Tour in 1975 by Bernard Thevenet.

Bernard Hinault scored five TDF wins between 1978 and 1985. His best chances of winning that elusive sixth came in 1980, when a knee injury forced him to abandon in the yellow jersey, and 1986, when he lost out to teammate Greg LeMond.

Winner from 1991 to 1995, Miguel Induráin became the first man to win the Tour de France five times in a row. He fell short in his bid to win a sixth in 1996.

## Who is the youngest Tour de France winner?

Henri Cornet was just a teenager when he won the second Tour de France in 1904. He was promoted from fifth to first after a spate of disqualifications, and he won the Tour at just 19 years and 352 days.

Grand Tour champions might be getting younger in the 2020s, but the record at the Tour de France has endured more than 120 years and will be difficult to beat even if current trends continue.

Tadej Pogačar is next on the list, winning the 2020 Tour de France when he was still a day short of his 22nd birthday.

Prior to Pogačar, Egan Bernal was the youngster Tour de France champion in over a century when he won the 2019 edition at 22 years and 196 days.

## Who is the oldest Tour de France winner?

Only rider over the age of 35 has ever won the Tour. Indeed, Firmin Lambot was 36 years old when he achieved the feat in 1923. In 2011, Cadel Evans became the oldest Tour winner since Gino Bartali in 1948 when he won the race at the age of 34 years and 160 days.

Bartali, meanwhile, achieved the remarkable feat of winning his second Tour a full decade after his first victory in 1938.
